opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really important question, because people sometimes frame it as language versus something else, as if a sufficiently powerful universal model would make language obsolete as an interface. I don't think that's how it plays out.

Language is a fantastic interface for certain things. It's incredibly efficient for communicating intent, abstract concepts, goals, constraints. If I want to say "make this scene feel more like late afternoon in autumn," that's a few words, and it carries a huge amount of information that would be really painful to specify any other way. That doesn't go away just because the model underneath becomes more general. In some sense, a more capable model makes language *more* useful, because it can do more with the intent you give it.

But language is also a lossy, low-bandwidth channel for a lot of things. If you want to describe exactly where an object sits in a 3D scene, or the precise shape of a curve, or how something should move, words are a really bad tool. You end up writing paragraphs to approximate what a gesture, a sketch, or just dragging something around would communicate instantly. Humans don't work purely through language either. An architect talks to a client, but they also sketch, build models, and point at things.

So when I picture a universal model, I don't picture one giant text box. I picture a model that understands many modalities natively, language, images, 3D structure, video, actions, and interfaces that let you use whichever one is most natural for what you're trying to express at that moment. Language stays as the layer for high-level intent and for explaining or asking about things, and spatial or visual interfaces handle the parts where you need precision and direct manipulation.

The other piece is that language is how we share things with other people, not only with machines. It's how we document, collaborate, and reason out loud. Even if the model could in principle read your mind through some other channel, a lot of the value of language comes from the fact that it's a shared, inspectable medium. That gives it real staying power regardless of what the underlying model looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says language is efficient for expressing intent and remains useful for shared communication, but it does not attribute that usefulness to people preferring to interact with systems through language.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, because the obvious prediction is that once you have a single model that handles vision, 3D, audio, video, everything natively, the text layer just becomes vestigial. And I actually don't think that's right. Language is the interface that humans have spent tens of thousands of years refining for compressing intent. When I want something, I don't have a precise 3D scene in my head or a pixel-exact image. I have a fuzzy notion, and language is the lossy-but-efficient way I externalize it. Whatever the model's internal representation looks like, I still have to get my intent into it somehow, and words are the highest-bandwidth channel I have that doesn't require me to be an expert.

The second piece is that language is where the specification lives. If you look at what we've been doing at World Labs with generating 3D worlds, the hard part isn't rendering the geometry. It's capturing what the person meant. "A cozy cabin, late afternoon, slightly abandoned" is doing an enormous amount of work in a very small number of tokens. A universal model might represent that internally as some continuous latent, but the handle you grab it by is still going to be linguistic, because that's the only abstraction both sides share.

And then there's the iteration loop. Once you have a draft, how do you steer it? You could imagine purely gestural or visual editing, and some of that will exist, but the moment you want to say "make it feel more like the second one but keep the lighting from the first," you're back to language. It's the glue between modalities. So my view is that the model becomes universal underneath, but language stays as the control plane, the way you point, specify, and correct. It just stops being the only thing the model can see.

r001.rationale: The response says language is an efficient way to express intent and steer systems, but does not attribute its continued usefulness to people preferring to interact through language.

astra-6.text:
I think even if you have a universal model underneath, you still need some way to tell it what you want. The model might understand images, video, audio, and actions, but that doesn’t mean it knows what you’re trying to accomplish at a particular moment. Language is a very flexible way of communicating that intent.

And it lets you operate at different levels of abstraction. You can give a broad goal, or you can get specific about a constraint, then refine it through a conversation. So I don’t think a universal model makes language interfaces obsolete. Language can be one of the ways we interact with that model, alongside showing it something or directly manipulating an object.

r001.rationale: The response says language is a flexible way to communicate intent, but it does not attribute language interfaces’ usefulness to people’s preference for interacting through language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language is still a really natural interface for telling a system what you want. Even if you have a universal model that can understand images, video, audio, and actions, it still needs to know your intent. You can show it a picture, but do you want it to describe the picture, edit it, or find something similar? Language gives you a flexible way to specify that.

So I don’t think a universal model makes language interfaces obsolete. It means you can combine language with other things—point at something, show an example, and explain what you want to change. The model can be much broader than language while language remains a useful way to communicate with it.

r001.rationale: The response calls language a natural, flexible way to express intent, but does not clearly attribute its continued usefulness to people’s preference for interacting through language.
